Barium chloride (BaCl₂) is formed.
HSO₄⁻ donates a proton (H⁺), forming SO₄²⁻; therefore, it acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid.
HCl is a strong, corrosive acid. The stomach lining protects the body from it, while the acid in the stomach helps digestion.
Soap is a sodium or potassium salt of a higher fatty acid.
Water can act as both an acid and a base: it can donate H⁺ or accept H⁺.
CO₃²⁻ accepts H⁺ from water to form HCO₃⁻, leaving OH⁻ ions in solution.
HCO₃⁻ can act as both an acid and a base: it can donate H⁺ to form CO₃²⁻ or accept H⁺ to form H₂CO₃.
A strong acid ionizes completely in water; a concentrated acid contains a large amount of acid per volume of solution.
An Arrhenius acid produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution, while an Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
Arrhenius acids produce H⁺ in water and Arrhenius bases produce OH⁻ in water. In the Brønsted–Lowry concept, acids donate H⁺ and bases accept H⁺.

MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O

A base reacts with a non-metallic oxide to form salt and water. This indicates that the non-metallic oxide is acidic.
HCl shows acidic character because it can donate H⁺ to a base. In water, it donates H⁺ to H₂O, forming H₃O⁺; in the gas phase, it can donate H⁺ to a suitable base such as NH₃.
An acid donates H⁺. Its conjugate base is the species left after that donation and can accept H⁺.
Acids have specific roles in the body: stomach HCl helps digestion, amino acids are building blocks of proteins, and fatty acids are components of lipids.
